title: Narrative Identity at Work in Digital Cultures: A Cultural–Analytical Psychological Framework
abstract: This article develops a cultural–psychological account of narrative identity at work in digital cultures. While narrative approaches have been central to understanding professional identity as a process of meaning-making, much existing research remains oriented toward language-centred and coherence-based models that offer limited resources for analysing work experience under conditions of digital mediation. Drawing on cultural psychology, narrative research, and studies of digital work, the article argues that digital work cultures reshape the conditions of narrative identity by intensifying regimes of visibility, evaluation, and recognition, while fragmenting professional experience across platforms and organisational contexts. Under such conditions, narrative identity cannot be understood solely through explicitly articulated self-stories. To address this limitation, the article advances a cultural–analytical framework that conceptualises narrative identity at work as a symbolically and affectively mediated process. While language remains central to narrative identity, the framework argues that explicit verbal self-narration does not exhaust it. Accordingly, it foregrounds symbolic forms, evaluative infrastructures, and affective orientations embedded in digital work environments as constitutive — alongside discourse — of professional meaning-making. Analytical psychology is mobilised as a cultural and symbolic resource, decoupled from its clinical origins. By reconceptualising narrative identity as a culturally mediated process embedded in digital work cultures, the article contributes to cultural–psychological debates on identity, work, and meaning-making.
